props.title: Aaron Loves Angela
props.initialSlug: Romeo and Juliet story set in Harlem

sections.content: **Aaron Loves Angela** (1975) stands as a vital but overlooked entry in 1970s urban romance, bringing Romeo and Juliet to Spanish Harlem with raw authenticity. Director Gordon Parks Jr., fresh off his success with **Super Fly** (1972), crafts a tender teenage love story between a Black basketball player and a Puerto Rican girl against the gritty backdrop of New York City's racial tensions. The film shares DNA with other significant 70s urban dramas like **Claudine** (1974) and **Cooley High** (1975), capturing both the energy and struggles of inner-city youth while avoiding exploitation tropes.

sections.content: The film's portrayal of interracial romance was groundbreaking for its era, predating similar themes in **West Side Story** (1961) but with a more grounded, contemporary approach. Kevin Hooks and Irene Cara deliver naturalistic performances that would influence later urban youth films like **Fame** (1980) and **Beat Street** (1984). Moses Gunn's portrayal of a local crime boss adds complexity to the narrative, reflecting the economic realities that complicated simple love stories in urban settings.

The film's soundtrack, featuring contributions from Jerry Peters and José Feliciano, creates a unique fusion of Black and Latin musical styles that perfectly captures the cultural intersection at the heart of the story. This musical approach influenced later films like **Krush Groove** (1985) and **Do the Right Thing** (1989) in their use of music to express cultural identity and community dynamics. sections.content: **Aaron Loves Angela** sits within a crucial period of Black cinema that moved beyond the limitations of Blaxploitation. Like **Thomasine & Bushrod** (1974) and **Mahogany** (1975), it attempted to tell more nuanced stories about Black life and love. The film's Spanish Harlem setting provides a realistic backdrop that would influence later New York-set romances like **Just Another Girl on the I.R.T.** (1992).
